clue.text: In sum, this disrupted narrow connection

indicators.note: disrupted means thrown into disorder, so the letters of sum and this are jumbled

explanation.surface: A summing-up: this broke the slender link.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disrupted' rearranges SUM + THIS; 'In' is only a link, though it tempts you to add its letters to the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: An isthmus is a narrow strip of land joining two larger land masses, such as Panama or Suez.

clue.text: Suffers retribution at first, framed by participant in hearing

indicators.note: only the first letter of the word before it is used

parts.note: the incus is one of the three small bones of the middle ear, all of which take part in hearing

indicators.note: the letter sits inside the next word like a picture in a frame

parts.note: its first letter, placed between INCU and S

explanation.surface: Someone at a court hearing is punished early on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' suggests a courtroom, and 'participant' a witness; it is the ear, and the participant is one of its bones.
explanation.definitionFit: To incur a penalty or a loss is to suffer it as a result of your own actions.

clue.text: Finally get wife, small figure, matching outfit

indicators.note: take the final letter of the next word

parts.note: its final letter
W = wife, as in genealogy tables
an inset is a small picture set into a larger one on a page

explanation.surface: A man eventually wins a wife with a small figure and dresses the pair alike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' suggests a body shape or a number; it is an illustration, and the small one inside a page is an inset.
explanation.definitionFit: A twinset is a matching cardigan and jumper worn together, a classic British women's outfit.

clue.text: I had to follow mark on gate for position in field

indicators.note: the piece comes after the next one

parts.note: M = mark, the old German currency
I'D is short for I had, placed after M
a wicket is a small gate, often set in a larger one

explanation.surface: Instructions for a farmer: I have to mark the gate that leads to a field.
explanation.walkthrough: The field is a cricket field, not a farm. Midwicket is a fielding position on the leg side, level with the middle of the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Midwicket is a named fielding position in cricket, so it is literally a position in the field.

clue.text: Provided with force after stone is difficult to move

indicators.note: the pieces before it come after the next one

parts.note: ST = stone, the British unit of weight
provided (that) means if
F = force in physics

explanation.surface: A heavy stone won't shift unless you push hard.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue order is misleading: 'after stone' means the first two words' letters come behind the stone, not before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiff hinge or lid is hard to move.

clue.text: Rustic youth backed the law with no limits

indicators.note: backed means turned back, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: a cub is a young person, as in a cub reporter or Cub Scout

indicators.note: without its limits, the first and last letters, the word loses both ends

parts.note: the law is a colloquial name for the police

explanation.surface: A country lad turned his back on the law, which knew no bounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' turns CUB into BUC; 'with no limits' strips POLICE to OLIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Bucolic describes the countryside and pastoral life, so it is a synonym for rural.

clue.text: Daughter comes in early when we are all thinking of sleep

definitions.text: when we are all thinking of sleep

indicators.note: the letter enters the next word

parts.note: betimes is an old word for early
D = daughter, placed after BE

explanation.surface: A daughter gets home early, just as the household is ready for bed.
explanation.walkthrough: BETIMES is old-fashioned but common in crosswords. The definition is a whole phrase describing the time of night.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedtimes are the times when people get ready to sleep.

clue.text: Witch left out of magic group

indicators.note: L (left) is removed from the next word

parts.note: the Magic Circle is the British society of magicians, so the group is a circle; its L goes

explanation.surface: A witch was thrown out of the magicians' club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left out' looks like being excluded; it strips the letter L from CIRCLE, leaving CIRCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Circe is the enchantress of the Odyssey who turned Odysseus's crew into pigs.

clue.text: Two supporters squeezing a beneficiary

indicators.note: the two outer pieces press in around the A

parts.note: a leg holds up a body or a table, and a tee holds up a golf ball
used as it stands, between LEG and TEE

explanation.surface: Two fans are crowding round the one who inherits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporters' look like fans; here they are things that hold something up.
explanation.definitionFit: A legatee is someone who receives a legacy under a will, a beneficiary.

clue.text: March off, insulting campaign to disarm

indicators.note: off in the sense of gone bad or wrong, so the letters of the word before it are in the wrong order

parts.note: taken as written
offensive means insulting, causing offence

explanation.surface: Someone is told to march off after an insulting attempt to win people over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' looks like part of march off, but it is the anagram signal on March alone; the next word gives a whole word on its own. 'disarm' is used in the sense of winning over hostile people.
explanation.definitionFit: A charm offensive is a deliberate drive to win people over by being pleasant, a campaign to disarm critics.

clue.text: Protect glass of wild creature joining party

indicators.note: the next piece is attached to this one

parts.note: a wild boar
the DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A wild animal has gatecrashed a party, so the windows need protecting.
explanation.walkthrough: The DUP is a real Northern Irish political party, fair game in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: To board up windows is to nail planks over them to protect the glass.

clue.text: Say lead time to go into cheap dinner

indicators.note: the letter is placed inside the next words

parts.note: base means cheap or low-grade, and a meal is a dinner
T = time, placed between ME and AL

explanation.surface: Someone says it's time to lead the way into a cheap dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say lead' reads as an instruction to go first; 'say' means for example, and lead is the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Lead is a base metal, a common one that corrodes, unlike gold or silver.

clue.text: A hard growth in fruit

parts.note: used as it stands
the hard, painful patch of skin that grows on a toe

explanation.surface: A hard lump has formed inside a piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit' suggests something sweet; the growth is a CORN on the foot, and the answer is the oak tree's fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanically the acorn is the fruit of the oak, a nut in a cup.

clue.text: All the representatives that can be contracted to Washington

definitions.meaning: every foreign envoy posted to one capital, taken together

definitions.text: that can be contracted to Washington
definitions.meaning: a phrase whose abbreviation is DC, the letters that follow Washington

explanation.surface: A group of lobbyists who might be hired to work in Washington.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contracted' looks like being hired; it means abbreviated, and Diplomatic Corps is abbreviated DC, the letters after Washington.
explanation.definitionFit: The diplomatic corps is the whole body of foreign ambassadors and envoys in a capital.

clue.text: China holds up definite examination

indicators.note: the first word has the next inside it

parts.note: china is rhyming slang for mate (china plate), so a pal

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means written from bottom to top

parts.note: definite means sure; written upwards as ERUS

explanation.surface: The Chinese government is holding up a final exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is not the country; in Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate.
explanation.definitionFit: A perusal is a careful reading through, an examination of a document.

clue.text: One who objects to young people shouldn't have this job!

definitions.text: One who objects to young people
definitions.meaning: the joke reading: someone who minds children, meaning dislikes them
the real sense: a person paid to mind, meaning look after, children

explanation.surface: A child-hater is in the wrong career.
explanation.walkthrough: To mind is both to object to and to look after; the clue uses one sense to hint at the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A childminder looks after other people's children in their own home for pay.

clue.text: Small jumper gripping person going round store

indicators.note: the first word surrounds the next

parts.note: someone who grasps, or grips
a store is a shop; it goes inside GRASPER after GRAS

explanation.surface: A little knitted sweater is clutching a customer walking round a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' looks like a sweater; it is anything that jumps. 'Gripping' is not the container word: 'going round' is.
explanation.definitionFit: A grasshopper is a small insect famous for its long jumps.

clue.text: Sage postpones opening of whiskey to the end

indicators.note: postponing the opening means the first letter is put off until later
that delayed letter goes to the end of the word

parts.note: Irish is a style of whiskey, spelt with the e as in Ireland

explanation.surface: A wise man waits until last orders to open his whiskey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'postpones opening of' and 'to the end' move the I of IRISH to the back. The spelling 'whiskey' hints at Irish rather than Scotch.
explanation.definitionFit: A rishi is a Hindu holy man or inspired poet, a seer of the Vedic tradition.

clue.text: Rapidly swallowing anger is most attractive

indicators.note: the first word takes the next inside it

parts.note: fast means rapidly
ire is anger; it goes inside FAST after FA

explanation.surface: Keeping your temper quickly makes you the most attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rapidly' is an adverb, and FAST can be one too: he ran fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Fairest is the old word for most beautiful, as in 'who is the fairest of them all'.

clue.text: Sign on motorway we think very important

indicators.note: in an across clue the piece is placed after the next one

parts.note: British motorways are numbered M1, M25 and so on
an omen is a sign of what is to come
in our view, or 'to us'

explanation.surface: A road sign on the motorway that we reckon matters a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign on motorway' reads as a road sign; it is OMEN placed after the M.
explanation.definitionFit: Something momentous is of great importance.

clue.text: Lose concentration and stop watching the dancing

definitions.meaning: the literal reading: a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A guest at a dance gets bored and looks away.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom comes from sport, but a ball is also a dance, so 'the dancing' gives a literal second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: To take your eye off the ball is to stop paying attention to what matters.

clue.text: Letter from joker not opened and not returned

indicators.note: the first letter is taken off
sent back, so written in reverse

parts.note: a comic tells jokes; without its first letter, OMIC
nor means and not; written backwards

explanation.surface: A card from a prankster that nobody opened or sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' looks like post; it is a letter of the Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Omicron is the fifteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, a short O.

clue.text: Getting into cabin maybe lifted me, arranging to have one new go

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted means written upwards, so me is read in reverse
one of the two letters is to go, so only a single one is lost
go means depart, so the letter is removed

parts.note: arranging is planning

explanation.surface: An airline passenger takes a new try at sorting out a lift into the cabin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifted' reverses ME to EM; 'to have one new go' drops one N from PLANNING to leave PLANING. A cabin is the passenger area of an aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: To emplane is to board an aircraft, so emplaning is going into its cabin, one example of a cabin.

clue.text: Stirs up old centres of population, bar one

indicators.note: except for one: the letter I is removed

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
cities are centres of population; without one I, CITES

explanation.surface: Someone stirs up unrest in the old cities, except one.
explanation.walkthrough: I = one, the Roman numeral, is what is barred.
explanation.definitionFit: To excite is to stir up feeling or activity.

clue.text: Polishes off ice creams, eating the whole amount

indicators.note: the first word takes the next inside it

parts.note: an ice cream in a cone is itself called a cone
the sum is the total; it goes inside CONES

explanation.surface: A greedy child finishes all the ice creams in one go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eating' fits the ice-cream picture but is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To consume is to eat or use up, so to polish off.

clue.text: Leave behind unfashionable sports clothes

parts.note: out of fashion is out
a team's strip is its playing kit

explanation.surface: Someone discards old-fashioned sportswear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave behind' looks like abandoning clothes; it means racing ahead. A strip is British for a team's kit.
explanation.definitionFit: To outstrip rivals is to move faster and leave them behind.

clue.text: Ranting etcetera out of place for British dramatist

indicators.note: out of place means in the wrong position, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A critic complains that ranting and the like are out of place on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of place' rearranges all fifteen letters of RANTING ETCETERA. Terence Rattigan wrote The Browning Version and The Winslow Boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Terence Rattigan was a twentieth-century English playwright, known for well-made plays like The Deep Blue Sea.

clue.text: Maybe a bishop is for everyone

indicators.note: maybe means perhaps, so the bishop is only one example of what is wanted

parts.note: used as it stands
the bishop is one of the chessmen, standing here for the whole class

explanation.surface: A bishop wants to belong to the whole flock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bishop' suggests a church; it is the chess piece, and 'Maybe' says it stands for any piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Apiece means for each one, as in 'they cost a pound apiece'.

clue.text: Endless additional period, over year, in great distress

indicators.note: the last letter is cut off
turned over, so written backwards

parts.note: extra means additional; without its end, EXTR
a period of time; written backwards as EMIT
Y = year

explanation.surface: A football match goes to extra time and runs over a year, to everyone's distress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Additional period' looks like extra time as one phrase; they are two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Extremity can mean a situation of great danger or distress, as in 'in their extremity'.

clue.text: Without easing up, losing the lead

indicators.note: the lead is the front position, so the word gives up its first letter

parts.note: slacking is easing up; drop the S

explanation.surface: A runner who lets up is losing the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: The racing picture of 'losing the lead' is exact: the first letter of SLACKING is lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking means without, as in 'lacking courage'.

clue.text: A variable number released from Berlin prison, potentially start of new life

indicators.note: the letters are let out of the next words

parts.note: a prison cell in Berlin is a German cell
A, and N for a variable number as in algebra; both are removed

explanation.surface: A number of inmates are freed from a Berlin jail and could start a new life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Released' fits the prison story; it strips A and N from GERMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A germ cell is a sperm or egg cell, which can go on to form a new organism.

clue.text: Unhelpful replies from one who is sent mad about step

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the word for step
mad means crazed, out of order, so the letters of the words before it are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
a stile is a step or set of steps for climbing over a fence

explanation.surface: A witness gives evasive answers, driven to distraction over a stile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent mad' reads as one phrase, but sent belongs to the fodder and 'mad' alone is the anagram signal; the stile, a step over a fence, sits whole inside the scrambled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In court a hostile witness is one who turns against the side that called them and gives unhelpful answers.

clue.text: Fasten bits back

indicators.note: sending something back returns it the way it came, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: bits are parts; written backwards

explanation.surface: Someone reattaches loose pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like putting bits back; it reverses them.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: you strap a suitcase shut or a child into a seat, securing it with a band.

clue.text: Sort of concrete play area since covered in part

indicators.note: the pieces are enclosed by the next word

parts.note: PT = part; it goes round RECAS
as means since, as in 'as it rained'
a rec is a recreation ground, a public playing field

explanation.surface: A playground was partly covered with concrete.
explanation.walkthrough: A rec is British shorthand for a recreation ground or park.
explanation.definitionFit: Precast concrete is moulded into blocks or panels before being brought to the building site.

clue.text: Spoil performance, introducing one crowd control measure

indicators.note: the first word brings the next one in

parts.note: to rot is to spoil
I = one, placed inside ROT
an act is a performance

explanation.surface: A heckler ruins a show, and stewards step in.
explanation.walkthrough: The Riot Act was a 1714 British law under which crowds could be ordered to disperse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Riot Act let magistrates order unruly crowds to break up, a measure of crowd control.

clue.text: One's entry into the race comes about by accident

definitions.meaning: the surface reading: someone joining a competition
the meant reading: this car only goes onto the track after a crash

explanation.surface: Someone ends up in a race by pure chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By accident' looks like 'by chance'; it means because of a crash.
explanation.definitionFit: In motor racing the safety car comes out after a crash to slow the field.

clue.text: Intensity of feeling to promote in the East End

indicators.note: the word is said in a Cockney accent

parts.note: to promote is to further; the East End of London accent turns TH into V

explanation.surface: Passion for getting ahead in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney, the accent of London's East End, says 'further' as 'furver'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: religious or patriotic fervour is emotion at a pitch of heat, from the Latin for boiling.

clue.text: A thousand invested in cash by obsessive for ground crop

indicators.note: money invested is put inside something

parts.note: cash is money
K = a thousand, as in a £20K salary; it goes inside MONEY
a fitness nut is an obsessive

explanation.surface: A fanatic puts a thousand pounds into a farm crop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invested' fits the money picture exactly. A monkey is also slang for £500, a trap to avoid.
explanation.definitionFit: The monkey nut, or peanut, ripens underground, so it is a ground crop.

clue.text: One blanket protects either side of engine in freeze

indicators.note: the covering word wraps round the next letter

parts.note: I = one
a blanket is a cover
its first letter, which is also its last, so either side gives it; put inside COVER after C

explanation.surface: A blanket keeps the car engine from freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: The blanket is a real winter trick for engines, but here it is just COVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that ices over freezes across its surface.

clue.text: Glacier mass would give anxiety with change of direction

indicators.note: a change of direction means the word is read the other way, backwards

parts.note: cares are worries, a form of anxiety

explanation.surface: A climber's dread grows as the path on the glacier shifts course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with change of direction' reverses CARES. A serac is a pinnacle or block of ice on a glacier.
explanation.definitionFit: A serac is a tall block or ridge of ice formed where a glacier's surface cracks.

clue.text: Leak suggesting diversion in volume?

definitions.meaning: the plain meaning: liquid escaping slowly
the joke reading: the two-word note in a book that sends the reader somewhere else

explanation.surface: A leak that sends water off in a new direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' looks like a quantity of water; it is a book, where 'see page 12' diverts the reader, and SEE PAGE run together is the leak.
explanation.definitionFit: Seepage is liquid slowly leaking through something.

clue.text: Comfortably settled, Charlie tucked into cake, in conclusion

indicators.note: the letter is put inside the next word

parts.note: the end is the conclusion

indicators.note: the whole goes inside the next word

parts.note: a scone is a small plain cake
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet, placed inside SCONE

explanation.surface: Charlie is sitting comfortably, eating cake, and that's that.
explanation.walkthrough: Two layers: C goes into SCONE, and the result goes into END.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone ensconced in an armchair is tucked in snugly and not about to move.

clue.text: Record man fighting against a roofed arcade

indicators.note: placed next to, so the pieces follow one another

parts.note: a log is a record, as in a ship's log
a GI is an American soldier
used as it stands

explanation.surface: A champion boxer takes on an opponent in a covered arcade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record man' reads as a record holder; the pieces split between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A loggia is a roofed gallery or arcade open on one side, common in Italian buildings.

clue.text: Huge couple of points short girl returned

indicators.note: cut short, so the last letter goes
sent back, so written in reverse

parts.note: a colon is two dots, one above the other; without its last letter, COLO
a lass is a girl; written backwards

explanation.surface: A girl came back two points short of a huge score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Points' suggests a score; they are the two dots of a colon.
explanation.definitionFit: Colossal means enormous, like the Colossus of Rhodes.

clue.text: Frequent subject for Matisse, nothing heartlessly Daliesque

parts.note: O, the figure nought, stands for nothing

indicators.note: heartlessly means the heart, the central letter of the word, is taken out

parts.note: the word as written, in the style of the painter Dali

explanation.surface: A critic judges a Matisse favourite heartless and very like Dali.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartlessly' removes the fifth of nine letters, the E in the middle of Daliesque. An odalisque is a harem woman, a recurring figure in Matisse's paintings.
explanation.definitionFit: Matisse painted many reclining odalisques, female slaves or concubines of a harem, so they are a frequent subject of his.

clue.text: Being around notes on and off someone in pink

indicators.note: the first word goes around the letters from the next

parts.note: a human being

indicators.note: switching on and off by turns, so letters are taken and skipped alternately

parts.note: every other letter, N-T-S, placed inside HUMAN

explanation.surface: A person wearing pink is surrounded by music.
explanation.walkthrough: Hunting pink is the traditional red coat worn by fox hunters, despite the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A huntsman on a British fox hunt traditionally wears a red coat called hunting pink.

clue.text: Don't be a hypocrite, and don't give impromptu lectures

definitions.meaning: the idiom: live by your own advice
the literal reading: rehearse your sermon before you deliver it

explanation.surface: Advice to a preacher about honesty and preparation.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes 'practise' as rehearse and 'preach' as lecture.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for living by your own advice, the opposite of hypocrisy; read literally, it means rehearsing a sermon.

clue.text: Fitness training hurt and told on one

parts.note: PE = physical education
ached means hurt

explanation.surface: A sore pupil after gym class tells tales on a classmate.
explanation.walkthrough: To peach is an old word for informing on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To peach on someone is to inform against them, to tell on them.

clue.text: Painkiller to sort out anyone discomforted in the head

indicators.note: in places the first letter of discomforted among the rearranged letters
to sort out means put into a fresh arrangement, so the letters of anyone are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here of discomforted

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A painkiller is wanted to help anyone suffering in the head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discomforted' tempts as the anagram signal, but it only gives its first letter; 'to sort out' is what rearranges anyone, and 'in' sets the D inside, after ANO.
explanation.definitionFit: An anodyne is a medicine that relieves pain, so a painkiller.

clue.text: Hotel New York Phil, for example, use frugally

parts.note: Hotel is H in the NATO alphabet
the New York Philharmonic is an American orchestra, a US band

explanation.surface: A hotel booking for the New York Philharmonic on a tight budget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Husband' is a verb here: to husband resources is to use them carefully.
explanation.definitionFit: To husband money or supplies is to spend them sparingly.

clue.text: Like a vampire, all but beneath notice

indicators.note: everything except the last letter

parts.note: beneath means under; without its last letter, UNDE
an ad is a notice in a paper

explanation.surface: A vampire, like everything else about him, is beneath notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All but' looks like 'nearly'; it cuts the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Vampires are undead: dead but still walking.

clue.text: No more visiting doctors with temperature

indicators.note: the next letter is added on

parts.note: someone visiting doctors is at the MOs, medical officers
T = temperature

explanation.surface: No more trips to the doctor once the fever is gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No more' looks like 'never again'; it means as a maximum. MO = medical officer.
explanation.definitionFit: At the most means no more than, as a maximum.

clue.text: Canvassed support?

definitions.meaning: the surface reading is election canvassing; the meant reading is 'fitted with a canvas'
the surface reading is political backing; the meant reading is a stand that holds something up

explanation.surface: A politician's campaign for backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canvassed' looks like election canvassing; here it means holding a canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: An easel is the stand that supports an artist's canvas.

clue.text: Physical unit of the past formerly found in the dictionary

indicators.note: the word sits inside the next one

parts.note: the OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
erst is an archaic word for formerly; it goes inside OED after O

explanation.surface: An obsolete unit of measurement once listed in the dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition includes 'of the past': the oersted is an old CGS unit, now replaced in SI.
explanation.definitionFit: The oersted is the old CGS unit of magnetic field strength, named after Hans Christian Oersted.

clue.text: Heard scoundrel try to be sick

indicators.note: we want the sound of the word, not its spelling

parts.note: a wretch is a scoundrel; the W is silent

explanation.surface: A rumour that a villain was trying to throw up.
explanation.walkthrough: WRETCH and RETCH are pronounced the same, since the W is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: retching is the heaving of the stomach as if vomiting, often with nothing brought up, so trying to be sick.

clue.text: Party food is cold, in short supply

indicators.note: Supplied short, the phrase hands over only a run of its letters, clipped at both ends.

parts.note: the letters run on unbroken across the words

explanation.surface: A complaint that the party food is cold and there isn't enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short supply' reads as scarce; it means only part of 'food is cold' is supplied, from its D to the CO of 'cold'.
explanation.definitionFit: A disco is a party with dancing to recorded music.

clue.text: Playwright's tips for writing with energy: cycling!

indicators.note: the letters go round, so the first letter moves to the end

parts.note: the tips of pens are nibs
E = energy; NIBSE then cycles its N to the end

explanation.surface: A playwright's advice: write with energy and go for a bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' looks like the bicycle; it moves the first letter round to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian playwright of A Doll's House.

clue.text: Porter was responsible for this classy group

definitions.meaning: Cole Porter, the American songwriter, wrote the score for a 1956 Bing Crosby and Grace Kelly musical film
the upper class, the fashionable set

explanation.surface: A hotel porter in charge of a posh party.
